summary: Describes how PIM can use a Join Attribute, from RFC 5384, to build multicast trees across an MPLS network even when the network's IGP has no route to the source. This is done with a Reverse Path Forwarding vector.

plainLanguage.summary:
Multicast traffic follows a tree of routers, and each router joins the tree by sending a Join message towards the source. The Join has to travel through every router on the path.

Some networks keep their core routers free of outside routes, so a core router cannot tell which way the source is. This document solves that by having the edge router name the exit point in the Join message, so the core routers forward it to that address instead of looking for the source.

how does pim work across an mpls core
what is a pim join attribute
why do core routers need an rpf vector
what is a bgp free core
subtitle: Lets PIM build a multicast tree across a core of routers that hold no routes to the multicast source.

tldr.problem: A network often keeps its core routers free of outside routes, so that only the edge routers know how to reach the rest of the Internet. That works for unicast traffic, but PIM needs every router in the path to send its Join towards the source, and a core router with no route to the source cannot do that.
tldr.mechanism: An edge router that knows the exit point adds a Vector Attribute to the PIM Join it sends into the core. The vector holds the IP address of the next edge router along the path to the root, and each core router does its reverse path forwarding check on that address instead of on the source address.
tldr.outcome: The multicast distribution tree can be built across a core with no external routes, for source trees and for shared trees alike. The attribute is a new type, value 0, in the PIM Join Attribute Types registry, and there is no way to carry it in a Bootstrap Router message.

facts.label: TLV flag bits
facts.value: F and S, one bit each

today: RFC 5496 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the value 0 in the PIM Join Attribute Types registry, and it builds on the PIM Join Attribute format of RFC 5384.

sections.title: The Problem With a Core That Holds No External Routes
sections.content:
It is sometimes convenient to distinguish the routers of a particular network into two categories: edge routers and core routers. The edge routers attach directly to users or to other networks, but the core routers attach only to other routers of the same network. If the network is MPLS-enabled, any unicast packet that needs to travel outside the network can be tunnelled via MPLS from one edge router to another. To handle a unicast packet that must travel outside the network, an edge router needs to know which of the other edge routers is the best exit point for that packet's destination IP address. The core routers, however, do not need any knowledge of routes that lead outside the network: as they handle only tunnelled packets, they only need to know how to reach the edge routers and the other core routers.

Consider the case where the network is an Autonomous System, the edge routers are External Border Gateway Protocol speakers, and the core routers constitute a BGP-free core. The edge routers distribute BGP routes to each other, but not to the core routers.

With multicast the strategy is more problematic. When using PIM Sparse-Mode, PIM Source-Specific Mode or Bidirectional PIM to create a multicast distribution tree for a particular multicast group, one wants the core routers to be full participants in the PIM protocol, so that multicasting can be done efficiently in the core. That means the core routers must be able to correctly process PIM Join messages for the group, which in turn means they must be able to send the Join messages towards the root of the distribution tree. If the root lies outside the network's borders and the core routers do not maintain routes to external destinations, the Join messages cannot be processed and the multicast distribution tree cannot be created.

The fix is a PIM extension. When an edge router sends a PIM Join message into the core, it MUST include in that message a Vector that specifies the IP address of the next edge router along the path to the root of the multicast distribution tree. The core routers can then process the Join by sending it towards the specified edge router, that is, towards the Vector. In effect, the Vector serves as an attribute, within a particular network, for the root of the tree. This document defines a new TLV in the PIM Join Attribute message of RFC 5384, consisting of a single Vector that identifies the exit point of the network.
sections.plainLanguage:
Some networks deliberately keep their core routers ignorant of routes outside the network. Only the edge routers know the way out. That is fine for ordinary traffic, which is tunnelled from edge to edge.

Multicast is different. Every router along the path has to send a Join message towards the source, and a core router that has never heard of the source has no way to choose a direction. This document gives the core routers a name to aim at.

sections.title: Building the Tree with a Vector
sections.content:
Before a router can start forwarding multicast packets, it is necessary to build a forwarding tree by sending PIM Joins hop by hop. Each router in the path creates forwarding state and propagates the Join towards the root of the forwarding tree. The building of the tree is receiver driven.

In the RFC's example, a source S sits behind edge router Edge 1 and a receiver R sits behind edge router Edge 2, with core routers between them. The two edge routers are BGP speakers, and the core routers are not BGP speakers and have no BGP-distributed routes. The route to S is a BGP-distributed route, so it is known to the edge but not to the core.

Edge 2 determines the interface leading to S and sends a PIM Join to the upstream router. In this example the upstream router is a core router with no route to S, so without the extensions in this document the core router cannot determine where to send the Join and the tree cannot be constructed. To let the core router take part, Edge 2 includes an RPF Vector TLV in the PIM Join Attribute of the PIM Join, and the TLV contains the IP address of Edge 1. Edge 2 forwards the PIM Join towards Edge 1, and each intermediate core router does its reverse path forwarding check on the address contained in the RPF Vector TLV, that is, on the IP address of Edge 1, instead of doing the check on the address S. That is what allows the tree to be constructed.

Whether an attribute is actually needed depends on whether the core routers have a route to the source of the multicast tree. How the edge router knows whether that is the case, and therefore how it decides whether to insert an attribute field, is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver asks to join a multicast group, and the request travels hop by hop towards the source. Each router that handles it creates forwarding state and passes it on. The core routers can pass it on only if they know which neighbour leads towards the source, and the vector tells them exactly that.

sections.title: Shared Trees and What the Extension Does Not Cover
sections.content:
The example above builds a source tree, to illustrate the attribute behaviour. The use of the attribute is not restricted to the construction of source trees. It may also be used to construct a shared tree, in which case the RPF Vector TLV contains the IP address of a Rendezvous Point. The procedures defined in this document for (S,G) Joins are equally applicable to (*,G) and (*,*,RP) Joins unless otherwise noted.

There is one thing the extension does not cover. There is no way to carry an RPF Vector TLV in a Bootstrap Router bootstrap message, and the procedures in this document do not define a way for BSR messages to be forwarded across a core in which the bootstrap router's IP address is not routable.
sections.plainLanguage: The same mechanism works for the other kind of multicast tree, where all receivers share one path to a meeting point called a Rendezvous Point. What it cannot do is help with the messages a bootstrap router sends to tell the network where that meeting point is.

sections.title: Processing a Received Vector Attribute
sections.content:
When processing a received PIM Join that contains a Vector Attribute, a router MUST first check whether the Vector IP address is one of its own IP addresses. If it is, the Vector Attribute is discarded and is not passed further upstream. Otherwise, the Vector Attribute is used to find the route to the source, and is passed along when a PIM Join is sent upstream.

A router that receives a Vector Attribute MUST use it, even if that router happens to have a route to the source. A router that discards a Vector Attribute MAY of course insert a new Vector Attribute, and this would typically happen if a PIM Join needed to pass through a sequence of edge routers, each pair of which is separated by a core that does not have external routes. In the absence of periodic refreshment, Vectors expire along with the corresponding (S,G) state.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router receives a Join carrying a vector, it first checks whether the address in the vector is its own. If it is, the vector is dropped, because the router has reached the exit point. Otherwise the router keeps the vector and passes it on with the next Join, even if it happens to know the route to the source itself.

sections.title: Asserts and Join Suppression
sections.content:
A PIM Assert message includes the routing protocol's metric to the source of the tree, and that information is used in the selection of the Assert winner. If a PIM Join is being sent towards a Vector rather than towards the source, the Assert message MUST have the metric to the Vector instead of the metric to the source. The Assert message itself has no attribute field and does not mention the Vector.

A router may change its upstream neighbour on a particular multicast tree as the result of receiving Assert messages. However, a Vector Attribute MUST NOT be sent in a PIM Join to an upstream neighbour that was chosen as the result of Assert processing, if that neighbour is different from the original upstream neighbour. Reachability of the Vector is only guaranteed by the router that advertises reachability to the Vector in its IGP, and if the Assert winner upstream is not the real preferred next hop, it is possible that the Assert winner does not know the path to the Vector. In the worst case the Assert winner has a route to the Vector on the same interface where the Assert was won, which points the RPF interface to that interface and results in the O-list being NULL. The Vector Attribute therefore MUST NOT be inserted if the RPF neighbour was chosen via an Assert process and the RPF neighbour is different from the RPF neighbour that would have been selected via the local routing table. In all other cases, the Vector MUST be included in the Join message.

Join suppression is the other place the vector matters. If a router receives a PIM Join on the upstream LAN interface for a particular multicast state, Join suppression may be applied if that Join is targeted to the same upstream neighbour. Which routers suppress their Join depends on timing and is unpredictable, and downstream routers on a LAN may include different RPF Vectors in their Joins. To make the upstream router's behaviour more predictable, the RPF Vector address MUST be used as an additional condition to the Join suppression logic: the suppression logic is applied only if the RPF Vector in the PIM Join matches the RPF Vector in the multicast state. It is also possible to disable Join suppression on that LAN.
sections.plainLanguage: Two other PIM features need care. An Assert message tells routers who has the better path to the source; when the Join is aimed at a vector rather than the source, the Assert has to carry the metric to the vector. And when routers on the same LAN decide whether to repeat a Join, the vector has to be the same on both sides, otherwise one router's Join could be suppressed on the basis of a vector that another router never sent.

sections.title: The Vector Attribute TLV Format
sections.content:
The Vector Attribute is a TLV in the PIM Join Attribute message, laid out like every other TLV: a byte of flags, a type byte, a length byte and a value.

The F bit is the Forward Unknown TLV bit. If it is set, the TLV is forwarded regardless of whether the router understands the Type; if the TLV is known, the F bit is ignored. The S bit is the Bottom of Stack bit: if it is set, this is the last TLV in the stack. The Type of the Vector Attribute is 0. The Length depends on the address family of the encoded unicast address. The Value is that encoded unicast address.

IANA has assigned the value 0 to the RPF Vector in the PIM Join Attribute Types registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The vector is carried as a small extra block inside the Join message, in the same way any other optional piece of information is carried there. It holds one address: the IP address of the exit point.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security of the RPF Vector Attribute is only guaranteed by the security of the PIM packet, so the security considerations for PIM Join packets as described in PIM-SM apply here.
sections.plainLanguage: The vector has no protection of its own. It is as trustworthy as the Join message that carries it, so the same protections that apply to PIM Join packets apply to it.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Bottom of Stack: this is the last TLV in the stack.
